transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-11
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Marc Ruiz (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Voyant Head of ML), Dmitri Ivanov (Voyant CTO), Samir Patel (Infra)

Summary (auto): Initial econ discovery; focus on unit cost, batching and caching levers, and deployment constraints (VPC, SOC2, KMS).
Topics: pricing per-token, dedicated pool vs hosted burst, prefix/KV cache savings, expected QPS, fallback routing, security and residency concerns.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alyssa Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um this is Alyssa from Redwood, i'll do a quick agenda — intros, current stack + goals, then Marc will walk through the levers (batching, cache, reserved capacity) and we'll leave time for q&a. sound good?
[00:08] Elena Park: yep thanks, i'm Elena. quick context — we run telematics inference for fleet routing, about 1.2M API calls/day today, each call is around 350 tokens average but we have peaks where sequences are longer, up to 6k tokens for multi-step session history. latency matter at edge, 95th needs to be < 300ms for most user flows.
[00:20] Dmitri Ivanov: and i'm Dmitri, CTO — our main question is do we go hosted for speed or negotiate dedicated reserved nodes, or bring Redwood private into our VPC. budget is tight — finance is looking at $/mile basically, so token burn matters.
[00:32] Alyssa Chen: great, good color. Marc, want to jump into the economics levers?
[00:35] Marc Ruiz: sure. um high level there are three places to influence unit economics — model selection/quantization, infra choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and software levers like batching and prefix / KV caching. I'll walk through typical numbers and tradeoffs.
[00:50] Marc Ruiz: (paraphrased) for hosted, our list example price is around $0.00045 per input token and $0.0009 per output token for the larger gen models — that's list, discounts apply. Dedicated reserved pools drop that by 30-60% depending on commit and burst profile. Private (customer-managed) removes our hosted unit charge but you carry infra & ops costs; in practice customers amortize to ~ $0.00015-0.0003 per token depending on utilization.
[01:16] Samir Patel: can you repeat that — the dedicated delta? our finance wants ballpark cost per 1M tokens.
[01:20] Marc Ruiz: yeah, so rough math — hosted list gives you predictable per-token billing. For dedicated, if you commit to a monthly pool — say a 4x A100 equivalent reserved cluster — your effective per-token can be 40% lower at steady state because you pay for capacity not per token. If utilization low you'll pay for idle. For Voyant scale, 1.2M calls/day and peaks, dedicated often makes sense after a certain threshold — we can model that in the spreadsheet.
[01:41] Elena Park: and the caching bit — we have long-running sessions with repeated prompts and a lot of telemetry-similar history. how much can caching save in practice?
[01:47] Marc Ruiz: prefix/KV cache is where we see big wins in chat-like or repeatable context flows. we typically see 30-60% token savings on retrieval-heavy flows; in telemetry where the first chunk is unique but later parts repeat, you could shave 40% average tokens. caveat: effectiveness depends on prompt entropy and how much of the sequence is prefixable.
[02:05] Dmitri Ivanov: important — does caching change latency SLOs? i.e., if a request hits cache vs cold model path.
[02:10] Marc Ruiz: good question. cache hits usually reduce latency because less compute needed; we serve cached KV entries from fast memory with almost no GPU decode. so p95 can actually improve for cached flows, but cache invalidation patterns matter. there is also complexity if you have strict residency / encryption requirements — keys are managed in KMS/HSM.
[02:28] Elena Park: what about batching — our QPS pattern is spiky during day shifts. batching helps cost but hurts tail latency, correct?
[02:33] Marc Ruiz: yes — continuous batching allows small waits to aggregate tokens into a bigger backend batch which raises throughput. We expose policy to control max batching latency. For example, batching window of 20ms could increase throughput 2x without hurting p95 too much; batching window of 80-100ms yields larger throughput but p95 will increase by that wait. For Voyant's 300ms p95 constraint, we can tune to stay under it while still gaining efficiency.
[02:56] Samir Patel: do you have a sample tradeoff curve? like cost per 1k requests vs p95 latency at different batching windows?
[03:02] Marc Ruiz: yes that's in the model we want to send; we'll run a custom curve based on your 8k seq worst-case distribution. the benchmark will produce throughput vs latency numbers at batching= [0ms, 20ms, 50ms, 100ms] and at batch sizes of 8/16/32.
[03:14] Alyssa Chen: quick qual question — where would you prefer model hosting? are you open to a staged approach (hosted pilot -> dedicated reserve -> private later)?
[03:21] Elena Park: staged is likely. legal wants to try hosted to move fast but infra wants VPC/private for compliance in the end. timeline: exec decision late Nov, procurement in Dec.
[03:32] Dmitri Ivanov: procurement will push for an SLA and audit logs, SOC2 type II and SSO/SAML we must have. encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS is a must for telemetry.
[03:42] Marc Ruiz: we support SSO (SAML/OIDC), SOC2, and KMS integrations for private and dedicated. Hosted also supports KMS-wrapped keys and audit logs — we'll bring our security pack to the next session.
[03:53] Elena Park: what about data residency — some of our fleets are in EU and APAC. If we host with Redwood, can routing be region-aware?
[03:59] Marc Ruiz: yes, smart routing by region is our standard pattern. hosted model endpoints can be pinned to region. With dedicated you can choose region-specific pools. For private on-prem we'd be within your VPC so data never leaves.
[04:12] Samir Patel: another ops question — do you maintain KV cache in the control plane or inside customer VPC for private deployments?
[04:18] Marc Ruiz: for hosted/dedicated, cache lives on the serving plane; keys and cache metadata are encrypted and we can offer customer-managed KMS for key material. For private, cache can be deployed in-customer VPC. There's an ops/complexity tradeoff there.
[04:30] Elena Park: pricing specifics — you mentioned discounts for commit, can you give a worked example for our volume? I'll throw numbers: 1.2M calls/day, avg 350 tokens in and 150 tokens out, so roughly 600M tokens/month.
[04:41] Marc Ruiz: quick calc — rough hosted bill at list: (600M * 0.00045) input + (600M * 0.0009) output = about $810k/month as a ballpark; with caching and quantization you could drop token consumption by 35% which would reduce that to ~ $526k. Dedicated reserved could drop unit rate by 40% so you'd be looking at $315k-$480k depending on utilization. These are illustrative — we'll model exact in the spreadsheet.
[05:12] Dmitri Ivanov: wow those numbers are big — finance will want to see mores sensitivity runs. do you support hybrid routing? like host lower lat flows and failover to dedicated?
[05:19] Alyssa Chen: yes hybrid routing is common — you can set policies by latency SLO, by customer tier, or route by region. automatic fallback to cheaper or more available model variants if primary is saturated.
[05:28] Elena Park: question on model quantization — will that impact output quality for our NLU tasks? we can't tolerate more than a tiny delta in fidelity.
[05:34] Marc Ruiz: quantization tradeoffs depend on model and task. we typically run eval suites on your prompts to measure delta; some 8-bit quantizations are nearly indistinguishable for many tasks, but for highly-sensitive NLU you'd want to validate. Redwood Optimize gives recommended quant profiles per workload.
[05:49] Samir Patel: for private deployment, what's the timeline to spin up an on-prem instance?
[05:53] Alyssa Chen: on-prem installs are heavier — typically 6-10 weeks for initial delivery + validation, shorter if you accept a hosted private VPC appliance which can be ~2-3 weeks. Dedicated pools are usually 2-3 weeks to provision with commit.
[06:05] Dmitri Ivanov: our other constraint is network egress cost — if we move telemetry to cloud, egress may spike. do you have guidance on co-locating models near data ingestion?
[06:12] Marc Ruiz: co-locating is recommended; dedicated pools in same cloud region as your ingestion cut down egress. For private you avoid egress entirely. We'll add egress sensitivity to the econ model.
[06:22] Elena Park: any hard limits on max sequence length? we said up to 8k in worst case.
[06:26] Marc Ruiz: we support up to 16k on selected model profiles and configured pools; larger context increases memory and cost but is supported. We have runtime kernel selection to optimize long seqs.
[06:35] Alyssa Chen: circling back — do you need a formal pilot to convince legal/security, or would a demo + security pack suffice to start procurement?
[06:42] Dmitri Ivanov: security will want an in-depth review; they'll likely ask for a pilot that includes audit logs and KMS proof-of-concept. so both.
[06:50] Elena Park: if we pilot hosted, is there a way to meter spend per team? we have multiple product teams using the same tokens.
[06:55] Marc Ruiz: yes token-level billing, per-token attribution in the console, and tagging. Redwood Console supports per-route dashboards, cost per token, and can emit usage hooks into your billing system.
[07:05] Samir Patel: operational question — do you expose KV cache invalidation controls? for us some telemetry must be purged rapidly.
[07:10] Marc Ruiz: yes you can purge keys, TTLs are configurable, and for private deployments you have full control. For hosted we offer APIs for fast invalidation along with audit logs.
[07:20] Alyssa Chen: ok we're at about 35 minutes in — any other top-level questions?
[07:25] Elena Park: one last thing — do you have customers with similar telemetry workloads? any case study?
[07:29] Alyssa Chen: we have a logistics customer who reduced token burn ~48% with prefix caching and batching; happy to provide a redacted case study.
[07:35] Dmitri Ivanov: last commercial question — how flexible are the commit terms if our usage grows or shrinks?
[07:40] Alyssa Chen: commits are usually 12-month with step-up/down options; we can model runway and add burst credits. We try to align with customer growth patterns.
[07:48] Marc Ruiz: technical wrap — i'll run the benchmark (8k seq profile, 0/20/50/100ms batching windows, batch sizes 8/16/32) and produce a throughput vs p95 curve plus estimated per-token cost under each deployment mode.
[07:58] Alyssa Chen: next steps recap — i'll send the pricing spreadsheet and unit-econ template, Marc will run benchmarks, Voyant shares prompt set and traffic sample, and we schedule security deep-dive.
[08:08] Elena Park: sounds good. target to have exec decision by Nov 30.
[08:12] Dmitri Ivanov: yes. thanks all.
[08:15] Alyssa Chen: great thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and calendar invites.

(Transcript notes: occasional word mis-transcriptions present — e.g., "KV" rendered as "K V" in some exports; product names sometimes lowercased; timestamps approximate.)
